title: Given a sorted array, a target value X, and a count K, find the K numbers closest to X. If two numbers are equally close, prefer the smaller. Explain how binary search locates X and a two-pointer window then selects the K closest.
shortTitle: K Closest Numbers (Find the K Elements Nearest a Target in a Sorted Array)
keyPoints: Binary search locates the target or its insertion point in the sorted array in O(log N) time.
Two pointers expand outward from the target position, always picking the closer side.
Because the array is sorted, the K closest elements always form a contiguous window.
The tie-break rule prefers the smaller number when two candidates are equally close.
Time complexity is O(log N + K) and space complexity is O(K) for the result.
A deque collects results in sorted order by adding left picks to the front and right picks to the back.

s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search to the target, then expand two pointers outward taking the closer side each time until K numbers are chosen.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **K Closest Numbers** is a Top K Elements problem that exploits the sorted order of the input array.
- **Binary search** finds the position of the target or its insertion point in O(log N) time.
- **Two pointers** straddle the target and expand outward, picking whichever neighbour is closer.
- The K closest elements always form a **contiguous window** in a sorted array.
- A **less-than-or-equal** comparison on the left side implements the tie-break preferring the smaller number.
- Time is **O(log N + K)** and space is **O(K)** for the result.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, interest-rate quotes from various lenders are stored in a sorted list. When Rajesh targets a particular rate for a customer, he needs the K quotes nearest to that target. He jumps near the target with binary search, then steps left and right, each time grabbing the side whose quote is closer, until he has K quotes to present.

sections.s6_takeaway:
K Closest Numbers finds the K values nearest a target in a sorted array, and the key insight is that the K closest numbers always form a contiguous window in sorted data. You do not need a heap. Binary search jumps to the target's position in logarithmic time, and then two pointers expand outward, one just left of the target and one just right, comparing distances and picking the closer candidate each time.

The tie-break is handled by the comparison operator: using less-than-or-equal on the left distance means that when two candidates are equally close, the smaller number is preferred. Collecting left picks at the front and right picks at the back of a deque keeps the result in sorted order without an extra sort step.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a rate advisory tool. When a customer targeted a particular interest rate, the tool presented the K nearest available quotes from a sorted quote board maintained by the treasury desk. The binary search plus two-pointer approach ran in O(log N + K) time, which was fast enough for real-time advisory sessions even with thousands of quotes.

The senior-level insight is recognizing that the K closest elements are contiguous in a sorted array, which lets you skip the heap entirely. Being able to explain why a heap is O(N log K) while the two-pointer approach is O(log N + K), and when each is appropriate, shows an interviewer you pick the data structure that fits the input.

Remember one sentence: in a sorted array, the K closest to a target form a contiguous window found by binary search plus two-pointer expansion.
